title: Project 2025 analysis warned of proposals to criminalize gender-affirming care
description_medium: A 2025 academic article analyzes Project 2025’s language about transgender people and its proposals concerning gender-affirming care. The authors argue that the agenda could expose trans people and care providers to criminalization. The cited material does not identify a federal prosecution of a student or family for supportive care, so the original title overstates what happened.
description_long: A 2025 article in Crime, Media, Culture examines how Project 2025 frames transgender people and gender-affirming care. The authors argue that its proposals could expand criminalization beyond trans people themselves to people who provide care, including therapists and doctors, and discuss the plan’s call for federal intervention against local officials who do not pursue certain criminal actions. Their analysis places those recommendations within a wider political effort to portray trans youth as a threat to children. This is an account of a proposed agenda and its possible legal consequences. It does not document a federal charge or prosecution of a student, parent, or family for supporting a transgender child. The entry’s original title presents such prosecutions as implemented policy, but the cited material supports a narrower description of the risks identified by the authors.

corrected_wording.title: Project 2025 analysis warned of proposals to criminalize gender-affirming care

source_access_notes: The SAGE article, NWLC report, and Transgender Equality state-of-schools page were retrieved. They describe proposed federal policy and existing state rules, not a documented federal prosecution of a family for gender-affirming support.
blockers: No federal charge or child-welfare case matching the title is identified in the cited material; evidence of an actual prosecution is needed to support that event claim.
rationale: States the supported action or policy proposal, attributes claims to the cited analysis, and separates proposals from implemented government actions.

title: Project 2025 proposed federal restrictions on LGBTQ+ content in schools
description_medium: PEN America’s analysis says Project 2025 proposed extending educational censorship through federal policy, including labeling LGBTQ+ content as pornography and treating librarians who provide it as criminals. The report also distinguishes these recommendations from book bans and restrictions enacted by states. It does not document a comprehensive federal ban or prosecutions of educators.
description_long: PEN America’s analysis of Project 2025 describes recommendations that could make educational censorship a federal policy. It highlights language characterizing LGBTQ+ content as pornography and argues that this framing could put librarians who provide such materials at risk of criminal penalties. The report also discusses calls to increase political control over education and to narrow the role of the Department of Education’s civil-rights office. These are recommendations in a policy blueprint, not proof that the federal government enacted a comprehensive ban on LGBTQ+ content in schools or media. PEN America separately describes state-level book bans and educational gag orders that were already affecting schools; those state actions should not be conflated with a nationwide federal prohibition. The National Women’s Law Center and National Education Association analyses likewise describe proposed changes to education and civil-rights policy. The evidence supports reporting a proposed federal censorship agenda and existing state restrictions, while the claim that federal law criminalized LGBTQ+ acknowledgment across media and schools goes beyond the cited record.

corrected_wording.title: Project 2025 proposed federal restrictions on LGBTQ+ content in schools

source_access_notes: PEN America, NWLC, and NEA analyses were retrieved. They discuss Project 2025 recommendations and state restrictions, not an enacted nationwide federal ban or completed prosecutions.
blockers: The cited materials do not identify an enacted federal ban, a federal monitoring system, or criminal cases against teachers or librarians for LGBTQ+ materials.
rationale: States the supported action or policy proposal, attributes claims to the cited analysis, and separates proposals from implemented government actions.

title: NIH terminated nearly 800 research projects as Trump proposed a major budget cut
description_medium: By April 2025, NIH had terminated nearly 800 research projects, according to a Nature analysis. Separately, the Trump administration proposed reducing NIH’s fiscal 2026 budget from about $47 billion to $26.7 billion and reorganizing its institutes. The budget was a proposal requiring congressional action, not an enacted $18 billion cut; the supplied sources do not document the claimed CDC program eliminations.
description_long: By April 2025, the National Institutes of Health had terminated nearly 800 research projects, according to a Nature analysis of federal grant data. Researchers described uncertainty and disruption as grants were canceled, including work in areas targeted by the administration. That action was distinct from the administration’s proposed fiscal 2026 budget: the plan reported by Science would reduce NIH funding by 44 percent, from roughly $47 billion to $26.7 billion, and reorganize its 27 institutes and centers into eight. The proposal also called for eliminating several institutes, including those focused on nursing, alternative medicine, minority health, and global health research. It still required congressional approval, so the proposed budget and reorganization should not be described as completed cuts. These facts support an account of actual project terminations alongside a major proposed reduction in NIH funding. They do not establish the title’s $18 billion figure as an enacted federal science cut, nor do the cited sources document elimination of CDC chronic-disease programs or the other sweeping effects asserted in the original description.

corrected_wording.title: NIH terminated nearly 800 research projects as Trump proposed a major budget cut

source_access_notes: Nature’s analysis, Science’s coverage of the FY2026 proposal, and STAT’s report on researcher experiences were retrieved. They support project terminations and a proposed NIH budget change, not the original enacted-cut and CDC claims.
rationale: States the supported action or policy proposal, attributes claims to the cited analysis, and separates proposals from implemented government actions.

title: Carter Page acknowledged contact with Russian deputy prime minister during Moscow trip
description_medium: Carter Page, a Trump campaign foreign-policy adviser, testified in 2017 that he briefly greeted Russian Deputy Prime Minister Arkady Dvorkovich during a July 2016 Moscow trip. Page initially said he had not met senior Russian officials, then described the contact. He also said he informed campaign staff about the trip; the record does not establish a deliberate cover-up.
description_long: Carter Page, an unpaid foreign-policy adviser to Donald Trump’s 2016 campaign, traveled to Moscow in July 2016 and delivered a speech at a university. In testimony later released by the House Intelligence Committee, Page said he briefly greeted Russian Deputy Prime Minister Arkady Dvorkovich. Reuters reported that Page initially said he had not met senior Russian officials, then qualified that account by describing the greeting. Page also testified that he told senior campaign staff about the trip, including Jeff Sessions, Hope Hicks, and Corey Lewandowski. The contact attracted scrutiny because Page advised the campaign on foreign policy during an election in which Russian interference was under investigation. The available reporting supports the trip, the meeting, and changing public descriptions of the contact. It does not by itself establish that Page concealed the meeting from the campaign or deliberately covered it up.

corrected_wording.title: Carter Page acknowledged contact with Russian deputy prime minister during Moscow trip

source_access_notes: Reuters and Guardian reports based on Page’s House Intelligence Committee testimony were retrieved. They document his acknowledgment and prior public account; they report that he informed campaign staff of the trip.
blockers: The supplied record does not establish intentional concealment or what Page disclosed to campaign officials about the Russian contact; the “covers it up” claim is unsupported.
rationale: States the supported action or policy proposal, attributes claims to the cited analysis, and separates proposals from implemented government actions.

title: Project 2025 proposed ending TPS protections for more than 850,000 people
description_medium: Doctors of the World’s analysis says Project 2025 proposed repealing Temporary Protected Status (TPS), which could strip legal protections from more than 850,000 people. That is a policy proposal, not evidence that all TPS designations had ended by September 2025. Secure Communities is a separate immigration-enforcement program; ICE says it was reactivated in 2017, not a humanitarian protection that Trump eliminated.
description_long: The cited Doctors of the World analysis describes a Project 2025 proposal to repeal Temporary Protected Status (TPS), which it says could affect more than 850,000 people living and working in the United States under that protection. This is a proposed change in the policy blueprint, not evidence that every TPS designation was terminated or that all affected people had already lost status. The original title also groups TPS with Secure Communities, but they are different programs: TPS protects people from designated countries from removal and authorizes work, while Secure Communities is an immigration-enforcement program that uses biometric data to identify people held by local authorities. ICE records that the program was suspended in 2014 and reactivated in January 2017. The supplied Project 2025 analyses discuss immigration proposals but do not document a 2025 elimination of Secure Communities or an across-the-board loss of status for 850,000 people. The supported account is therefore a proposed rollback of TPS protections, with the separate enforcement program identified accurately.

corrected_wording.title: Project 2025 proposed ending TPS protections for more than 850,000 people

source_access_notes: Doctors of the World and archived ICE Secure Communities pages were retrieved. The Civil Rights PDF link returned no readable text in the scrape; the packet notes that its cited materials describe Project 2025 proposals rather than completed terminations.
blockers: The cited sources do not establish which TPS designations were terminated, when any changes took effect, or that 850,000 people had already lost status by September 2025.
rationale: States the supported action or policy proposal, attributes claims to the cited analysis, and separates proposals from implemented government actions.
